## Box Room Home Office Ideas UK: 14 Space-Saving Setups

URL: https://britishhomeinterior.co.uk/blog/small-home-office-ideas-uk/

A UK box room — typically 6–8 sqm, often irregularly shaped, sometimes windowless — can genuinely work as a home office. The constraints are real: limited floor space, limited natural light, and (in rented properties) limited ability to modify the walls. But those constraints are solvable with the right desk, the right storage approach, and better lighting.

This guide focuses on setups that work for UK box rooms specifically: the desk options that fit in a narrow room, the lighting that compensates for no window, and the storage that doesn't require drilling.

For the broader box room picture — using the space as a bedroom or nursery instead — see [small box room ideas UK](/blog/small-box-room-ideas-uk).

---

## The Box Room Desk Decision

The desk takes up the most space, so it's the first decision.

### Option 1: LINNMON 100x60cm + ALEX Drawers (~£100–£140, IKEA)

The standard small-home-office setup for a reason. The 100cm width fits along most box room walls without crowding the door. The 60cm depth gives enough space for a monitor at a proper viewing distance. The ALEX pedestal drawers add storage without adding a second piece of furniture.

**Works for:** rooms that are at least 1.8m wide after the desk is placed, with a chair pulled out.

### Option 2: Wall-mounted fold-down desk (~£40–£120)

The best option for the smallest box rooms (under 6 sqm) or for anyone using the room as a combined bedroom-office. When the desk is folded up, the floor is completely clear. Most can hold a monitor, keyboard, and laptop when open.

B&Q, Wayfair, and Amazon UK all stock fold-down wall desks. Renter note: these require screwing into the wall — get written permission first, or ask the landlord to install one (some will, if framed as a permanent improvement).

**Works for:** rooms under 2m wide, or where the space doubles as a bedroom.

### Option 3: Corner desk (only in a square room)

Corner desks only make sense when both walls are the same length and the room is genuinely square. In a typical UK box room — often rectangular or with a sloped ceiling on one side — a corner desk wastes more space than a straight desk, because one arm is unusable and one arm blocks the door or window.

**Works for:** perfectly square rooms of at least 2.5m × 2.5m.

---

## Storage Without Drilling

UK renters need storage that doesn't require wall anchors or permanent fixtures.

**KALLAX 2×2 cube unit (~£45, IKEA)** — 77cm wide × 77cm tall. Sits beside or behind the desk. Deep enough for A4 box files and storage boxes. Can double as a second monitor stand if the top surface is at the right height.

**Desk-top monitor riser with drawer (~£20–£40, Amazon)** — raises the monitor to eye level and adds a slim drawer for cables, stationery and hard drives. Saves a significant amount of desk surface.

**KALLAX fabric inserts (~£6 each)** — turn open cube shelves into closed storage. Useful for keeping the room from looking cluttered during video calls.

**Over-door organiser (~£10–£20)** — the back of the box room door can hold a pocket organiser for notebooks, stationery, and small items. Most over-door products hook without damaging the door.

**Cable management box (~£8–£15, Amazon)** — keeps the extension lead, charger cables, and cable excess inside a single box on the desk or floor. The single most visible improvement to make a box room look like a proper office rather than a storage room with a desk.

---

## Lighting for a Box Room

Lighting makes or breaks a windowless box room office.

**Overhead LED:** replace the existing bulb with a cool-white 4000K LED at the maximum wattage the fitting allows. Most UK box rooms have a single ceiling light — one good bulb does a lot.

**Desk lamp with daylight bulb (5000–6500K):** a second light source aimed at the desk surface eliminates shadows when working. Look for a lamp rated at 400+ lux at desk level — this is often listed in the product description on Amazon or John Lewis.

**Monitor bias lighting (~£10–£15):** an LED strip behind the monitor reduces eye strain in a dark room by increasing the ambient light level behind the bright screen. USB-powered, no installation needed.

Avoid warm-white bulbs (2700K) as the only light source in a windowless office — they create an orange-yellow cast that makes the room feel like a bedroom, not a workspace.

---

---

## Chair Options for a Box Room

The chair is often where box room offices fail — a large executive chair can make a 7 sqm room feel like an obstacle course.

**MILLBERGET (IKEA, ~£99)** — narrow profile, adjustable height, no armrests option available. The most practical ergonomic chair for a small room.

**FLINTAN (IKEA, ~£79)** — even slimmer than MILLBERGET. Good for rooms under 2m wide.

**Kneeling chair (~£40–£80)** — zero width behind the desk. Promotes better posture for under 4 hours per day; not a full-day solution.

**Folding chair:** the cheapest option and genuinely fine for part-time home working. An IKEA TERJE (~£30) folds flat against the wall when not in use.

---

## Video Call Backgrounds in a Box Room

The box room home office is visible in video calls, which matters if you're on calls frequently.

**The cheapest fix:** face the door (plain wall behind you) rather than facing the window (bright background that silhouettes you).

**Practical setups:**
- Place a small bookcase with neat books behind you
- A plain light-coloured wall with one framed print
- A ring light or LED panel in front of you — fills in shadows and makes a windowless room look bright on screen

**Avoid:** a cluttered shelving unit, laundry, or door visible behind you. A virtual background is a last resort — they pixelate on slower connections and look unprofessional if the background detection is poor.

---

## Renter Checklist Before Setting Up

1. **Check for a phone line or ethernet port** — many UK box rooms have neither; check if you need a powerline adapter or MoCA adapter to get a wired internet connection without running a cable down a hallway
2. **Count the plug sockets** — a UK box room often has one double socket; an extension lead with surge protection is the first purchase
3. **Note ceiling height on the sloped side** — many UK box rooms are under a staircase or roofline; confirm you can sit upright where the chair will be
4. **Test the door swing** — ensure the desk position allows the door to open fully; a desk that blocks the door is a building regulation issue in some tenancy agreements
5. **Check the heating** — box rooms often share a radiator with a hallway or have no radiator; a small electric panel heater (~£30–£60) is the renter-friendly solution

## 11 Small Living Room Ideas UK

URL: https://britishhomeinterior.co.uk/blog/small-living-room-ideas-uk/

The average new-build living room in the UK measures around 17 square metres — and many older flats, particularly in London and other major cities, are significantly smaller than that.

This guide covers visual tricks — colour, curtains, mirrors, rug size — and they matter most in a *very* small living room, the kind you find in a one-bed flat or a 1930s semi. For furniture arrangement and floor plans specifically, see [Renter-Friendly Living Room Layout Ideas UK](/blog/renter-friendly-living-room-layout-ideas-uk/).

We're working with less space than almost any other European country. And most advice about "making rooms feel bigger" was written for spaces that are already considerably larger than most British flats.

Here's what actually works.

**TL;DR:** The most impactful small-room tricks are ceiling-height curtains, furniture with visible legs, correctly sized rugs, a large mirror opposite the window, and a light-neutral wall colour. Together these can make a small British living room feel genuinely spacious — not just less cramped.

---

Read more: [renter-friendly living room layout ideas UK](/blog/renter-friendly-living-room-layout-ideas-uk/)

## 1. How Do You Hang Curtains to Make a Small Room Feel Taller?

No single change does more for the perceived height of a small room than curtains hung near the ceiling rather than the window frame. The eye follows the fabric from floor to ceiling and reads the room as taller. The window also appears much larger, and more light enters.

A repositioned curtain pole costs as little as £8 for a new IKEA RÄCKA pole, or nothing if you already own a drill — a small, renter-friendly change that measurably increases how tall a small room reads.

The curtains should be wide, too — extending 15–20cm past the window frame on each side so that when fully open, they sit almost entirely off the glass. This reveals the full window and maximises the natural light that a small room depends on.

If your current curtain pole is mounted at window height, moving it up may simply require repositioning the existing brackets — a 30-minute job with a drill. If you're in a rented property, check your tenancy agreement before drilling new holes.

Curtain pole repositioned near ceiling — free if you have a drill, or ~£8 for a new IKEA RÄCKA pole.

---

## 2. Why Does Furniture With Visible Legs Make a Room Feel Bigger?

Skirted sofas and chairs — those with fabric or material going down to the floor — visually block the floor and make a room read as heavier and more cramped. Sofas and chairs raised on legs, even short ones, reveal floor beneath them. Your eye sees more floor and the brain registers more space.

Swapping a skirted sofa for a raised-leg model — such as the IKEA Söderhamn at roughly £499 — reveals visible floor beneath the seating and makes a small room read as noticeably more open, without changing its actual footprint.

This applies to coffee tables and side tables too. A glass or acrylic coffee table top on slim metal legs shows the maximum floor area. A solid wooden cube does the opposite.

The sofa is only slightly smaller in footprint but the visible floor beneath it transformed the room.

Sofa with visible legs — IKEA Söderhamn from ~£499 at IKEA.

---

## 3. Where Should You Place a Mirror in a Small Living Room?

In a small room, a large mirror does two things: it bounces natural light deeper into the space, and it creates the visual impression of a second room beyond the wall. Both effects make the room feel significantly larger.

The mirror should be statement-sized — at least 60–80cm wide — to have real impact. Position it opposite or at a 45-degree angle to the main window. Leaning it against the wall rather than hanging it creates a more casual look and avoids renter complications.

Round mirrors are particularly good in small rooms because they avoid competing with the room's angular architecture. Dunelm's [round mirror](https://link.amazon/B0118Gors) range starts at ~£25 and includes excellent large-format options.

Large round mirror — from ~£25 at Dunelm.

---

## 4. What's the Right Rug Size for a Small Living Room?

The instinct in a small room is to use a small rug. This is almost always wrong. A rug that's too small for the furniture arrangement makes the room feel more chaotic, not more spacious — the furniture floats without anchor and the space reads as undefined.

Sizing up from a 90x120cm rug to a 160x230cm one, available from around £45 at Dunelm, is what actually grounds a small room's furniture arrangement rather than fragmenting it.

The correct minimum in even a small UK living room: at least the front legs of all seating should sit on the rug. This grounds the arrangement and tells the eye "this is the room." A 160x230cm rug in a small space reads as intentional and considered; a 90x120cm rug floating in the middle reads as an afterthought.

The correctly sized rug paradox: in a small room, the correctly sized rug makes the room feel bigger than a smaller rug, because it defines the space rather than fragmenting it visually.

Correctly sized rug 160x230cm — from ~£45 at Dunelm.

---

## 5. Use Warm Neutral Paint — Not Stark White

Many people assume white is the best colour for a small room. In UK conditions, this is often wrong — particularly in north-facing rooms, where natural light is limited and cool throughout the day. Stark white in low UK light reads as grey, flat, and slightly cold.

Warm neutrals like Dulux Goose Down, at around £22 for 2.5L from B&Q, avoid the flat, cold cast that stark white takes on in low, north-facing UK light.

Warm neutrals — Dulux Goose Down, Crown Fossil, Farrow & Ball Pavilion Grey (which despite its name reads very warm) — work better. They add warmth, they read as brighter than they are because warm tones respond well to lamplight in the evening, and they don't draw attention to the room's limited size the way that a very particular or saturated colour might.

Warm neutral paint — Dulux Goose Down ~£22 per 2.5L from B&Q.

---

## 6. Why Use Floating Shelves Instead of Floor Units?

Bookshelves and storage units that sit on the floor add to the visual mass of a small room. Floating shelves mounted on the wall preserve floor area and draw the eye upward, making the ceiling feel higher.

Floating shelves start at around £8 per shelf for IKEA's LACK range, with wider B&Q options from £15, giving a small room storage and visual interest without occupying any floor space.

In a small living room, a grid of floating shelves on one wall — styled with books, plants, and objects — creates significant storage and visual interest without occupying any floor space at all. IKEA's LACK [floating shelves](https://link.amazon/B05CaPemG) are the most reliable budget option at ~£8 per shelf. B&Q has wider and deeper floating shelf options from ~£15.

Renters: floating shelves require wall fixings. Check your tenancy agreement — some landlords permit shelving with written approval, especially if you agree to fill the holes on exit.

Floating shelf — IKEA LACK from ~£8 at IKEA.

---

## 7. What Size Sofa Works Best in a Small Living Room?

In a small living room, sofa scale matters more than almost any other furniture decision. A large three-seater or sectional sofa in a small room dominates the space and leaves little room to move. A two-seater or compact three-seater at the right depth (typically under 90cm deep from front to back) allows the room to breathe.

A compact sofa under 90cm deep, such as options from Next Home starting around £299, lets a small living room breathe in a way a standard-depth three-seater can't.

Standard UK sofas are often too deep for small living rooms. Look for sofas described as "apartment" or "compact" sizes — Dunelm and Next Home both label these clearly. A [slim side table](https://link.amazon/B02l54C6E) (~£25-£40) pairs well beside a compact sofa. Pair with a single armchair for flexibility without bulk.

Compact two-seater sofa — from ~£299 at Next Home.

---

## 8. Use Nesting Tables Instead of a Coffee Table

A fixed coffee table in a small living room takes up floor space permanently. Nesting tables — typically a set of two or three tables that stack together — take up the footprint of one small table when nested and spread out to serve multiple purposes when needed.

A set of nesting tables from around £35 at Dunelm or Wayfair takes up the footprint of a single small table when stacked, freeing floor space a fixed coffee table would otherwise claim permanently.

They're particularly useful for small flats where the living room doubles as a dining space, or where you regularly have people over. When nested, the floor area they reveal makes the room feel considerably more open.

Dunelm and Wayfair both stock nesting tables from ~£35 per set.

Set of nesting tables — from ~£35 at Dunelm.

---

## 9. What TV Size Is Right for a Small Living Room?

An oversized television in a small living room dominates the space visually and forces furniture to be positioned further back than the room allows. A screen that's too large for the viewing distance (less than 1.5x the screen diagonal for comfortable watching) also creates eyestrain.

For the typical 2-2.5 metre sofa-to-TV distance in a small UK living room, a 43-50 inch screen is the proportionate choice — anything larger dominates the room without improving the viewing experience.

For a small UK living room with a typical sofa-to-TV distance of 2–2.5 metres, a 43–50 inch screen is the right proportion. Going larger doesn't improve the experience — it just makes the screen more visually dominant when switched off.

Correct TV size for small rooms: 43–50 inches at 2–2.5m viewing distance.

---

## 10. Use a Single Pendant or Picture Light Over the Sofa

Rather than relying on a central ceiling rose (which draws the eye to the middle of the ceiling and makes the room feel boxier), use a pendant hung low over a side table, or a picture light mounted on the wall, to create lighting that exists at a lower level and adds depth rather than overhead glare.

A plug-in pendant light from around £22 at Dunelm creates lower, warmer lighting than a central ceiling rose, without any rewiring — making it renter-friendly too.

Plug-in pendant lights — which don't require rewiring and work in rented properties — are available from Dunelm from ~£22. These hang from a ceiling hook (which can be adhesive in plaster ceilings) and the cord runs to a wall plug.

Plug-in pendant light — from ~£22 at Dunelm.

---

## 11. Edit Aggressively

In a small living room, every item either earns its place or makes the room feel smaller. Editing — removing objects that don't actively serve the space — is the final and often most powerful technique.

No new purchases were involved; editing is often more effective than any purchase.

The test: does this object make the room better to be in, or does it just exist? Scatter cushions beyond four, decorative objects beyond the rule-of-three groupings, side tables without clear purpose, and floor items that could be shelved — all of these should be considered for removal.

Cost: nothing. Set aside an hour to edit without adding anything.

---

## How Big Is the Average UK Living Room?

The average new-build living room in the UK is around 17 sq m (183 sq ft) — but that number hides a huge range. Victorian terraces often have front rooms of 12–14 sq m, while 1930s semis can be 18–22 sq m. Flats built after 2010, especially in London and other cities, are often smaller still.

Understanding your actual room size helps calibrate expectations:

| Room Size | What to Expect |
|---|---|
| Under 12 sq m | Very tight. Two-seater sofa max, no coffee table (use nesting tables), wall-mounted everything. |
| 12–16 sq m | The most common small UK living room. Compact three-seater or two-seater, one side table, floating shelves. |
| 16–20 sq m | Still compact but workable. Room for a three-seater, coffee table, and a small TV unit. |
| Over 20 sq m | Not small by UK standards. Most layout and space-saving tricks still help but aren't essential. |

Measure your room before making any decisions. A tape measure and a quick sketch save you from buying furniture that doesn't fit — the single most expensive mistake in a small living room.

## North-Facing vs South-Facing: Why It Matters in the UK

UK rooms face a problem that southern-hemisphere and equatorial countries don't: directional light that changes everything about how a room feels.

**North-facing rooms** get no direct sunlight. They tend to feel cold, flat, and grey — especially in winter. The fixes:
- Use warm-toned paint (Dulux Goose Down, Farrow & Ball Joa's White) rather than cool greys or bright whites.
- Maximise artificial warmth with lamps at multiple levels — table lamps, floor lamps, wall lights.
- Place mirrors to bounce whatever light enters deeper into the room.

**South-facing rooms** get direct sunlight for most of the day. These rooms can handle cooler tones and darker colours without feeling oppressive — a small south-facing room in a deep green or navy can feel genuinely luxurious.

**East and west-facing rooms** get morning or afternoon sun respectively. Work with the light you get: warm colours in east-facing rooms (which lose sun by afternoon), and cooler tones in west-facing rooms (which get warm afternoon light).

## Small Living Room Storage That Doesn't Look Like Storage

In a small living room, every visible surface should either be useful or beautiful — ideally both. The best storage in a small room is invisible:

- **Ottoman with hidden storage** — replaces a coffee table, holds blankets and remote controls. Dunelm has several from ~£60.
- **TV unit with closed cabinets** — hides cables, games, and clutter. A unit with doors rather than open shelves keeps the room looking calm.
- **Console table behind the sofa** — thin enough to not take walkway space, wide enough to hold a lamp and a few books.
- **Baskets under side tables** — a woven basket under a side table stores magazines, chargers, or throws without looking cluttered.

For the full guide to storage furniture that hides everything, see [Renter-Friendly Living Room Layout Ideas UK](/blog/renter-friendly-living-room-layout-ideas-uk/).

## Where to Shop for Small Living Room Furniture in the UK

Not all UK retailers stock apartment-size furniture. These do:

- **IKEA** — the widest range of compact furniture in the UK. The SÖDERHAMN, KIVIK, and FRIHETEN sofas are all available in apartment sizes.
- **Dunelm** — rugs, mirrors, nesting tables, and cushions at prices that make sense for a small room.
- **Made.com** — modern compact sofas and shelving, with dimensions clearly listed.
- **Habitat** — small-space-friendly designs, especially for side tables and coffee tables.
- **Argos** — budget furniture that ships fast. The Home collection has several compact ranges.

For bedroom-specific furniture in a small flat, see [Small Bedroom Ideas UK](/blog/small-bedroom-budget-uk/). For the whole-flat approach, [renter-friendly living room ideas UK](/blog/renter-friendly-living-room-ideas-uk/) covers deposit-safe changes.

| 4 | Replace coffee table with nesting tables | ~£35–£60 |
| 5 | Check rug size — upgrade if too small | ~£45–£80 |
| 6 | Apply warm neutral paint | ~£22–£35 |
| 7 | Add floating shelves to replace floor units | ~£8–£25 |

## Small Utility Room Ideas UK

URL: https://britishhomeinterior.co.uk/blog/utility-room-ideas-uk/

Most utility room ideas you find online show a room the size of a small bedroom, with a butler sink, a boot bench, and a dog-washing station. That is not the UK utility room. Here, a utility room is usually a cupboard off the kitchen, a slice of the garage, a lean-to at the back, or — for a lot of renters — no room at all, just the washing machine wedged under the kitchen [worktop](/blog/budget-kitchen-cabinet-makeover-uk/) and an airer that lives permanently in the hall.

A good utility zone does four jobs — house the appliance, give you a surface to fold on, dry a load without taking over a room, and hide the cleaning kit — and you can fit all four into a 60cm cupboard if you plan it in the right order.

This guide covers the small and awkward versions: the utility cupboard, the corner-of-the-kitchen conversion, and the renter setup that needs no building work at all.

Read more: [kitchen on a budget UK](/blog/kitchen-on-a-budget-uk/) for the same space-first approach applied to the kitchen itself.

> **Key Takeaways**
> - Four jobs, in order: appliance, folding worktop above it, a drying rail, closed storage for cleaning kit.
> - A 60cm laminate worktop offcut over the machine (from £25 at B&Q) is the single highest-value change.
> - A drop-down or retractable drying rail (£12–£30) replaces a floor airer and frees the floor.
> - Renters can build the whole thing freestanding — slimline unit, over-door rail, lidded baskets, no drilling.

---

## How Small Can a Utility Room Actually Be?

A utility room needs about 1.5 to 1.8 square metres to work as a room — space for the appliance, a worktop above it, and enough clearance to open the door and stand in front of the machine. Below that, stop thinking "room" and start thinking "cupboard."

A utility cupboard is a 60cm-wide unit, deep enough to take a washing machine (so at least 60cm deep, ideally 65cm), with the machine at the bottom, a fixed shelf or two above, and a folding or curtained front. In a UK terrace or a flat, this is often the only realistic option, and it works fine — nationally described space standards for new homes don't require a separate utility room at all, which is why so few flats have one.

The one measurement that matters most: leave at least 50cm of clear floor in front of the machine so the door opens fully and you can crouch to load it. Everything else can be tighter than you think.

![A compact utility room with a plywood worktop over a front-loading washing machine and open shelving below the sink](/images/utility-room-uk.jpg)

## What's the Right Layout for a Small Utility Room?

Work bottom to top, wet to dry. Appliances and plumbing at floor level, a continuous worktop over them at 90cm, storage above that, and drying provision hung from the wall or ceiling rather than standing on the floor.

The order to fit things in, when space is tight:

1. **The washing machine**, against the wall with the plumbing, at floor level.
2. **A worktop over it** at standard 90cm height — this is the folding surface, and it hides the machine's top. A 60cm laminate offcut from B&Q or Wickes costs £25–£40 and can simply rest on the machine and an end support if you're renting.
3. **A drying rail** — drop-down, retractable, or a ceiling airer (a Sheila Maid pulley airer, from £45, is the traditional UK version and uses only ceiling space).
4. **Closed storage above the worktop** for detergent, cloths, and the iron — a wall cabinet or a covered shelf, so it isn't all on show.
5. **A tall, narrow gap** somewhere for the ironing board and the vacuum — even 20cm beside a unit is enough if you add a bracket or a tension rod to stop them falling.
6. **A bin**, ideally wall-mounted or on the back of the door.

If you have a dryer as well as a washing machine, **stack them** with a stacking kit (£25–£40, check it matches both brands) rather than losing a second run of floor to a side-by-side pair.

## How Do You Turn a Kitchen Cupboard Into a Utility Room?

Take one run of full-height units — the tall larder cupboards, ideally near the back door or in a corner — and gut the inside. Washing machine at the bottom, worktop over it, shelves above, a rail for drying, and a bifold door or a curtain to close it off.

This is the standard fix for UK homes with no separate room, and it's how most "utility room" makeovers in flats and terraces actually happen. A few specifics that make it work:

- **Keep the cabinet doors if they match your kitchen** — a bifold pair folds flat against the side and doesn't swing into the room. If they don't match, a floor-to-ceiling curtain on a ceiling track costs under £30 and hides everything instantly.
- **Run the worktop through** at the same height and material as the rest of the kitchen so the cupboard reads as part of the room, not a bolt-on.
- **Put a strip light under the top shelf** — these cupboards are always dark, and a £15 battery or plug-in LED strip makes it usable.
- **Line the back wall** behind the machine with a wipeable panel or even a tile sheet — it takes the splashes and looks finished when the door's open.

## What Can Renters Do Without Building Anything?

Everything above has a freestanding version. A slimline shelving unit beside the washing machine, a worktop offcut resting (not fixed) on top of the machine, an over-door drying rail, and a set of lidded baskets covers the same four jobs with no drilling and nothing that breaches a standard tenancy's original-condition clause.

The renter kit, with real UK prices:

- **[Slimline shelving unit](https://link.amazon/B0fRt4dKP)**, 30–40cm deep, from £20 at IKEA (the JOSTEIN or IVAR frames) or Wilko — holds detergent, spare bedding, and cleaning kit.
- **Worktop offcut or a chopping-board-style top**, £15–£30, laid across the machine for folding.
- **Over-the-door drying rail**, £12–£20 (Minky, Addis) — hangs a full load on the back of any door.
- **[Lidded storage baskets](https://link.amazon/B0imtehX9)**, £6–£12 each (Dunelm, B&M) — closed storage so it doesn't look like a jumble.
- **A tension rod** across a narrow alcove, £8, to corral the ironing board and mop.

Total: £70–£110 for a working utility zone that comes apart in ten minutes on moving day. See [kitchen on a budget UK](/blog/kitchen-on-a-budget-uk/) for the same reversible approach across the rest of the kitchen.

![Storage baskets on a shelf keeping utility clutter contained](/images/bathroom-storage-baskets-shelf.jpg)

## How Do You Make a Utility Room Look Good?

Paint it a real colour, add closed storage, sort the lighting, and treat the floor. A utility room is the one place in the house where a deep, practical colour genuinely works better than white — it hides scuffs from the mop and the laundry basket, and it makes a small windowless room feel intentional rather than forgotten.

What actually changes how it looks, for under £60 total:

- **Colour**: a deep green (Farrow & Ball Green Smoke, or B&Q's own-brand equivalent), a clay/terracotta, or a warm off-white — not brilliant white, which shows every mark. One tester and a small tin covers a cupboard or a tiny room.
- **Closed storage**: get the detergent bottles and the yellow-and-green packaging out of sight. Decanting into plain bottles or just using a lidded basket does it.
- **Lighting**: swap the bare bulb for a warm 2700K one, or add a battery wall light if there's no fitting. A windowless room lit with cold light always looks grim.
- **Floor**: a washable runner or a coir mat over whatever's there. Vinyl click flooring (from £15/m² at B&Q) over old lino if you own it.
- **One framed print** on the back wall. It sounds pointless in a utility room. It isn't — it's the difference between "storage" and "a room."

## Utility Room Ideas by Space: A Quick Reference

| You have | Best setup | Rough cost |
|---|---|---|
| A separate small room (1.5m²+) | Machine + dryer stacked, full worktop run, ceiling airer, wall units above, painted colour | £150–£400 DIY |
| A tall kitchen cupboard | Gut it: machine, worktop through, shelves, bifold door, strip light | £80–£200 |
| A corner of the kitchen | Slimline unit beside the machine, worktop offcut on top, over-door rail, curtain to hide | £70–£130 |
| A hallway or under-stairs cupboard | Shelving for cleaning kit + linen only (no plumbing), tension rod for airer | £40–£90 |
| Renting, can't drill | All freestanding: slimline unit, resting worktop, over-door rail, lidded baskets | £70–£110 |

---

The utility room is proof that in a UK home, planning beats square footage. A cupboard laid out in the right order — appliance, worktop, drying, closed storage — does everything a proper room does, and a coat of dark green paint makes it look like you meant it.
